title: PM Modi Urges All Parties to Back 33% Women's Reservation in Parliament
excerpt: The Prime Minister appealed for cross-party support to operationalize the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, warning that four decades of political delays on women's representation must end.
body:
• PM Modi appealed to all political parties to vote in favor of operationalizing 33% women's reservation in Parliament and state assemblies
  • The government introduced three bills including the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill to fast-track the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam for 2029 elections
  • The Delimitation Bill proposes increasing Lok Sabha seats from 543 to approximately 850, with women's reserved seats potentially added as additional seats
  • The NDA holds 293 seats but needs a two-thirds majority of 360 seats, requiring opposition support to pass the constitutional amendments

Prime Minister Narendra Modi made a direct appeal to opposition parties to support the operationalization of 33% women's reservation in Parliament and state legislatures, calling on lawmakers to set aside partisan politics on an issue that has been delayed for nearly four decades.

The Legislative Push

The government introduced three bills in the Lok Sabha: the Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026, which provides 33% reservation to women in Parliament and state assemblies; the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, extending the quota to Delhi and Jammu and Kashmir; and the Delimitation Bill, which proposes increasing and redrawing Lok Sabha constituencies to approximately 850 seats.

https://x.com/MeghUpdates/status/2088511033946382706

The bills aim to fast-track a 2023 law — the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam — that mandated one-third reservation for women in legislative bodies but lacked an implementation timeline. The government has set its sights on making the quota effective from the 2029 general elections.

"For four decades, a great deal of politics has been played on the issue of women's reservation in the country. Now is the time that half the country's population must certainly receive its rights."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi

Modi's Appeal to the Opposition

With the ruling National Democratic Alliance holding 293 seats — short of the 360-seat two-thirds majority needed to pass constitutional amendments — the Prime Minister directly addressed opposition leaders. He urged them to vote with "complete sensitivity" and warned against actions that could hurt the sentiments of India's women.

Modi framed the legislation as a collective achievement for India's democracy rather than a partisan victory. He argued that history would judge Parliament not by party lines but by whether it delivered on a promise pending since the women's reservation bill was first proposed decades ago.

The Prime Minister also pushed back against demands for sub-quotas within the reservation framework — including for Muslim women and women from backward classes — saying the Constitution does not permit lawmakers to "think in fragments." National decision-making, he said, must remain inclusive and uniform.

The Delimitation Question

While broad bipartisan support exists for putting more women into Parliament, the linked Delimitation Bill has generated friction. The proposed increase from 543 to about 850 seats would trigger a sweeping redrawing of voting boundaries.

Opposition parties have raised concerns that the boundary changes could tilt the political balance in favor of the BJP, particularly at the expense of southern states like Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Goa, which have performed well in family planning and fear losing representation.

To address this, Modi said the government would provide a legislative assurance that no state would lose Lok Sabha seats due to population control efforts. Women's reserved seats may be created as additional seats, expanding the overall strength of both houses rather than displacing existing representation.

A Historic Gap

Women currently hold only about 14% of seats in the lower house of Parliament. India already mandates one-third reservation for women in local governance bodies — panchayats and municipal councils — but that quota has never extended to higher legislative levels.

Modi pointed to the growing political consciousness among women who have participated in panchayati raj institutions over three decades, saying they now expect representation in national policy-making.

"If we move forward together, history will not favour any one political side. It will stand with India's democracy."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi

The bills require a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament to pass. With debate continuing into the early hours, the outcome will depend on whether opposition parties join the government in backing one of the most consequential shifts in political representation since India's independence.
